title: Through the Lens: Nepal, one month after the floods - Nikkei Asia
description: Through the Lens: Nepal, one month after the floods  Nikkei Asia
publisher.title: Nikkei Asia
full_article:
BIDUR, Nepal -- Saturday marks one month since massive floods and landslides devastated parts of Nepal. More than 7,000 people have been killed or remain missing, according to the latest figures from the country's disaster authority, while damage and economic losses are estimated at about $2.7 billion.

Signs of exhaustion are increasingly visible among those who lost family members and homes. But, while many remain displaced and face an uncertain future, communities are slowly trying to reclaim a sense of normalcy. Memorial gatherings have been held to mourn the dead, while schools are gradually reopening and classes resuming in flood-hit communities.

Walking through the Devighat area of Bidur in central Nepal on the morning of Sept. 21, the stench was strong as sludge and sodden debris baked in the hot sun. The weather on Aug. 26, the day the Trishuli River flooded, was similarly clear.

The once-colorful streets of Bidur, downstream from some of the worst-hit areas, have given way to a gray landscape. Muddy floodwaters rose as high as the third floor of buildings, sweeping away even reinforced concrete structures and leaving those still standing badly damaged.

Even so, residents were quietly shoveling mud from their homes in a city that has become a key hub for relief efforts and displaced people.

All photos and video by Ken Kobayashi.

Nabin Chitrakar shovels sludge from his home.

Collapsed buildings, mangled trees and twisted steel rods lay embedded in the mud around him. Chitrakar had run a small shop selling supplies to pilgrims visiting the nearby Jalapa Devi Temple. About 30 minutes before the flood struck, he loaded some valuables into a car and drove uphill, warning others along the way to flee.

The flood erased the boundary of his family's compound and engulfed the house, carrying mud and debris to the upper floors. A storeroom in the backyard, where the family kept sacks of grain and a washing machine, was destroyed. After spending three weeks in tents amid persistent rain and poor sanitation, the six family members began taking turns clearing the property themselves.

Sarita Tamang and Kanchhi Maya Tamang mourn their mothers

A pair of girls stood in front of tents erected as temporary shelter in Bidur on Sept. 20.

Sarita Tamang, 18, said she had just arrived at school with her 16-year-old friend Kanchhi Maya Tamang when a teacher told them a flood was coming and shouted at them to run. The two quickly fled up a mountain. After hearing that villages upriver were already washed away, Sarita called her mother, but got no response.

"We saw it from the hill," Sarita said. "The water swallowed up the streets, everything. We couldn't do anything but cry."

Both girls' mothers died in the disaster.

"Right now, there's nothing I want," Sarita said. "I can't even think about the future."

Buddhist monk Karma Tsegyal offers prayers

The disaster-hit area runs along a 1,000-year-old trade route between Tibet and Nepal. Tibetan Buddhist temples are a common sight, and Buddhism is a major religion in the region.

Karma Tsegyal, a 45-year-old Buddhist monk of the Kagyu school, had been praying at an altar in Bidur when he heard a strange roaring sound from the river. When he looked over, he saw the mudslide rushing along, engulfing houses as it went.

Dozens of photos of the deceased are now displayed at Tsegyal's temple, many of them members of the Tamang people from the mountains of central Nepal. Among them is a picture of Sarita's mother.

"We will pray for those who died, and for those who survived," Tsegyal said.

Aite Bishwakarma vows to live for his grandchildren

Aite Bishwakarma, 58, stood atop a hill at Trishuli in Bidur that had escaped the damage, overlooking the river. His eldest son, 33-year-old Raju, remains missing.

Raju had been hired as a truck driver just three months earlier, crossing the border with Tibet and bringing back products from China.

On the morning of the flood, Raju got in touch with his wife. He has not been heard from since.

"He was apparently near the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, where the damage was worst," Bishwakarma said.

"I don't think my son will come back," he added quietly.

Reality has left little time to grieve. With his son's wife and three children having lost their breadwinner, Bishwakarma is supporting them himself.

"I'm going to go back to work making farming tools," he said. "My daughter-in-law might leave, but I'm going to live for my grandchildren. Even if I have to beg, I want to survive and bring them up well."

Nepal prime Minister Balendra Shah on Thursday warned the United Nations General Assembly about the devastating impact of climate change. He said catastrophic floods that killed at least 1,400 people in the country highlighted the human cost of a crisis borne most severely by those least responsible for it.Addressing the UN General Assembly, Shah said the crisis was not limited to Nepal and pointed to the wider impact of climate change and conflict across South Asia."We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food. And this is not Nepal’s private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh, ask Bhutan, ask India, ask the Maldives, ask Pakistan, ask Sri Lanka, ask any other country in our region and you’ll hear the same account."Shah said Nepal and other countries in the region were facing the consequences of crises they had not caused."Hit by the climate we did not warm and again hit by the wars we did not start," said Balen Shah.More than 6,000 people remain missing, while the damage is estimated at around 10 per cent of Nepal’s gross domestic product (GDP).“The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world,” he said. “And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?”Shah said the warming climate was destabilising the Himalayan ecosystem, with melting permafrost making mountain slopes increasingly unstable and raising the risk of avalanches, floods and landslides.He added that the devastation extended across Nepal’s border with China and downstream into India.“Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports," Shah said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 5,130 people remain missing, while 13,728 people have been rescued so far. Only 104 bodies have been identified and handed over to their families. Meanwhile, 339 people are undergoing treatment in 19 hospitals, while 3,761 displaced people are staying in 37 holding centres.

title: A month after Nepal floods, thousands are still missing and families face a long recovery - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: A month after Nepal floods, thousands are still missing and families face a long recovery  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- After spending five years working in Saudi Arabia, Narayan Prassan returned to his home in Nepal with savings, only to lose his house in the 2015 earthquake. He went abroad again, earned enough to rebuild his home and settled happily with his family.

Last month’s floods have destroyed everything once more.

With his home in a designated danger zone and no clear idea of where his family will resettle, Prassan is staying with his wife and children at a relative’s house and mulling another stint overseas.

“This flood has taken everything,” he said. “I don’t know what to do.”

A month after devastating floods swept through parts of Nepal, thousands are displaced like Prassan and rescuers continue searching for thousands others missing, including many believed trapped in six hydropower project tunnels. The disaster has left the government facing a long and costly recovery, with families confronting the loss of loved ones, homes and livelihoods.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah used his first address to the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday to highlight the flooding as a warning about the growing climate risks facing the Himalayan region.

“The disaster was not just a local tragedy, but a warning to the world,” Shah said. “I ask you today: Have we really heard that warning?”

Shah also called for greater international support for Nepal’s recovery and stronger regional cooperation to prepare for climate-related disasters.

“Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports,” he said.

Nepal’s disaster management agency said 1,453 bodies had been recovered and 5,644 people remained missing. Only 112 bodies had been handed over to relatives, while 1,333 were temporarily buried pending identification. In neighboring China, officials reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing.

Tents have been set up at the Nepal Police Hospital in Kathmandu, where relatives can provide DNA samples to help identify the dead. Authorities are comparing the samples with DNA collected from recovered remains.

Laboratory officials declined to provide details, citing privacy concerns, but said experts from India, China, the United States, Singapore and South Korea were assisting with the work.

Rabi Kumar Thapa Magar, a hydropower worker who lost his wife, brother, sister-in-law and mother, said he identified his wife from a photo of the dead — but authorities had buried her body before the family could see it.

Authorities declined to release the body pending DNA matching, a process they said would take at least a month. The family later performed symbolic final rites using an effigy.

Many others are still processing the grief.

Pasang Maya Tamang, 32, who lost her young son in the floods, said she still dreams of him pleading for help.

“The body of my son has been recovered but I was not able to see him for the last time. I am very sad about that. I hear in my dreams him saying why I left him alone,” Tamang said at a shelter home in the flood-affected town of Nuwakot.

Her son had gone to school with a neighbor when the flood hit. By the time she learned what had happened, the school had already been swept away. His body was recovered three days later in a southern district, but she was unable to travel there to see him.

The Aug. 26 flood hit in the morning, around the time students were arriving at schools or making their way there. Some children's bodies were later recovered still wearing ties bearing their school’s logo, said Asta Man Dangol, a resident in Nuwakot.

"The older students were able to run uphill and escape, but the little ones who were not able to run fast ... were swept away," he said.

The Nepal government estimates reconstruction and recovery will cost $4.77 billion. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected, and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed.

The recovery is now focused on restoring roads and bridges cut off by the floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made it difficult to deliver aid.

Ishmita Shah, a roads engineer, said crews have been working with Nepal's army since the second day after the floods to reopen routes in affected areas.

Shah said bridges were being built to improve access to the worst-affected areas and make it easier to transport relief supplies. But the work remains difficult, with more bad weather expected in the coming days, she said.

“The upcoming few days are going to be very challenging because of the weather, but we are fully prepared for that too,” she said.

title: Landslide kills one as heavy rain disrupts life across Nepal - kathmandupost.com
description: Landslide kills one as heavy rain disrupts life across Nepal  kathmandupost.com
publisher.title: kathmandupost.com
full_article:
A 69-year-old man died after a landslide buried his house in Baglung district on Friday night, as heavy rain continued to disrupt life across Nepal on Saturday, inundating settlements, triggering evacuations and blocking roads in several districts.

Man Bahadur Roka was sleeping on the porch when the landslide came down from above and buried him in Dhammer, Tarakhola Rural Municipality-5, police said. He died at the scene. His father, Salle Roka, was away at his daughter’s home and was unharmed. Roka’s wife and children lived in a separate house.

In Nawalparasi West, more than 200 houses in the Susta settlement of Susta Rural Municipality-5 were inundated after the Narayani river overflowed. The river had initially flooded the Tharu settlement on Friday, but rising water levels later inundated much of Susta.

About 400 residents have been moved to a disaster-management shelter, according to Chief District Officer Dipak Raj Nepal. Security personnel, including Nepal Police and Armed Police Force teams, have been deployed for rescue and evacuation operations.

The Narayani river was also approaching the danger level. At 4am on Saturday, the water level at the Devghat gauge had risen to nearly 8 metres. The warning level is 7.3 metres, while 9 metres is considered the danger level.

At the Gandak barrage in Tribeni, the water level had risen to 376,800 cusecs by 10:30am, according to the water measurement centre. All gates of the barrage were opened as the flow increased.

Evacuations in Butwal

In Rupandehi, 20 families living along the Tinau river in Butwal were moved to a local school after the river crossed its warning level.

The affected families, who had been living beneath the Tinau bridge, were taken to Kanti Secondary School, according to police. Several settlements along the river, including Majuwa, Buddha Nagar, Devinagar and Raniganj, remain at high risk as the water level continues to rise.

Roads blocked by landslides

In Baglung, three days of continuous rain triggered landslides and brought traffic on major roads to a halt. A landslide at Kanabagar in Nisi Khola Rural Municipality-4 blocked the Mid-Hill Highway, with authorities using an excavator to clear vehicles trapped in mud.

Other sections of the highway were also affected by smaller landslides and muddy roads. Long-distance vehicles have been barred from operating in the district since Thursday night.

In Gulmi, landslides have blocked three major roads—the Kaligandaki Corridor, Madan Bhandari Auxiliary Highway and Ridi-Rudrabeni road.

Rising water in the Kaligandaki river also forced seven families in Ridi to move to relatives’ homes.

Authorities have banned all vehicular movement as heavy rain, blocked roads and rising river levels increased risks across the district.

Tourist site, bridge affected

The rising Kaligandaki river has inundated parts of the Rani Mahal area in Palpa and put the historic palace at risk. About half a dozen hotels, resorts and shops in the popular tourist area have been flooded, according to local officials.

In northern Gorkha, flooding in the Therang Khola damaged a wooden bridge linking Namrung in Chumanubri Rural Municipality-4 with Bharjam in ward 2. A landslide fell about 10 metres above the bridge on Saturday morning, damaging the structure along the Manaslu trekking route.

In Pokhara, the Seti river has formed a temporary lake at Ramghat after its flow increased and a narrow outlet restricted the river’s passage. The Kaski district administration has urged residents in riverside areas to remain alert.

Power supply disrupted

Heavy rain and falling trees have disrupted electricity supplies in Palpa, where the Butwal-Palpa, Gulmi-Palpa and Syangja-Palpa 33-kV transmission lines have been affected.

In Dadeldhura, a sal tree brought down by strong winds and persistent rain obstructed the Budar-Jogbuda 33-kV transmission line, disrupting power supplies in the Jogbuda area. Nepal Electricity Authority officials said repair teams were struggling to reach the site because swollen streams and unsafe roads had made access difficult.

Authorities have urged people living along rivers and in other vulnerable areas to remain alert as rainfall continues and water levels are expected to rise further.

Both families identified the body as their next of kin based on characteristics such as clothing and physical features.

However, the fingerprint comparison conducted by Yong and his colleagues showed that the body did not belong to either family.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Corelle Tan, a senior investigation officer with the Criminal Investigation Department, was part of the team involved in lifting fingerprints from the bodies.

"When we arrived, it had already been about a week since the disaster.

"So a lot of the bodies and remains were in an advanced state of decomposition, as some of them were soaked in water and mud."

Tan said they had to adapt, as some of the methods they learnt during their training could not be used.

This process involves documenting and examining the bodies for any distinguishing features to help identify the deceased. These include gender, estimated age, tattoos, moles and scars.

"One of the challenges was the scale and condition of the bodies, which had differing degrees of decomposition and trauma. This can make the identification process difficult," Kuek said.

Thousands of grieving Nepalis are still struggling to come to terms with the scale of the losses caused by last month's catastrophic floods, which tore through the Nepal-Tibet border and left widespread devastation in their wake.

The deadly floods in Nepal's Bhote Koshi River on 26 August killed at least 1,453 people and left more than 6,000 others, including hundreds of foreign nationals, missing.

Those still missing include 33 Britons, 80 Americans, more than 50 Ukrainian nationals, as well as Australians and Indians, with most presumed to have been swept away by the tsunami-like waves that destroyed towns and villages in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

The other 1,333 bodies founds so far have been temporarily buried pending identification. In neighbouring China, officials reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing.

Pramod Poudel, 34, from Uckfield in East Sussex, said he does not believe his missing family members will be found. He travelled to Nepal to join the search after losing contact with his wife Sumitra, mother Tulisa, brother Pardip and uncle Madhav.

He told BBC News: "My heart is still saying that there might be something there, but I have to be realistic and accept that they are not there anymore.

Nepal's government is also struggling to re-home and provide support to an estimated 33,000 displaced people, many of whom have spent the past month in tents at rehabilitation shelters.

Pasang Maya Tamang, 32, who lost her young son in the floods, said she still dreams of him pleading for help.

"The body of my son has been recovered, but I was not able to see him for the last time. I am very sad about that. I hear in my dreams him [asking] why I left him alone," Mr Tamang said at a shelter home in the flood-affected town of Nuwakot.

Forty-seven bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites, according to reports.

The floods severely damaged Nepal's hydropower sector, a crucial driver of economic growth and an increasingly important source of export revenue.

Aid agencies have warned that further heavy rainfall forecast in the coming days could increase the threat of landslides, making it harder for help to reach areas where roads have already been damaged by the floods.

"It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty."

Ishmita Shah, a roads engineer, said crews have been working with Nepal's army since the second day after the floods to reopen routes in affected areas.

Ms Shah said bridges were being built to improve access to the worst-affected areas and make it easier to transport relief supplies. But the work remains difficult, with more bad weather expected in the coming days, she said.

description: 'Nepali Diaspora, a crucial pillar of Nepal's development journey'  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Sept 26: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has described the Nepali diaspora as a crucial pillar of Nepal's development journey. He emphasized the need for further contributions from this community toward the country's progress.

Interacted with members of the Nepali diaspora in New York earlier today, Minister Khanal emphasized the need to integrate the knowledge, skills, experience, capital, and networks of Nepalis residing in various countries with Nepal's development. He stated that the government is committed to collaborating with the diaspora more effectively and enhancing their contribution to national development priorities, according to the Foreign Minister's Personal Secretariat.

Minister Khanal is currently in New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

At the event organized by the Consulate General of Nepal in New York, representatives from the diaspora delivered presentations on topics such as technology, artificial intelligence (AI), disaster management, and the potential contributions of the diaspora to Nepal's development, the Secretariat reported.(RSS)
